label: Traditional Chaldean cyclical planetary hour ordering
claims: method
first hour begins Sun-rise
The first planetary hour of every day starts at local sunrise.
Not midnight-based 60-minute civil-hour segmentation.
method
first hour assigned Planet of the day
The planetary ruler of the weekday governs the first daylight hour.
Links weekday to first planetary-hour position.
method
second hour next Planet
The second hour goes to the next planet in the cyclic traditional order.
The order is not weekday sequence.
method
Sun Venus Mercury Moon Saturn Jupiter Mars
The underlying hourly succession on Sunday is Sun, Venus, Mercury, Moon, Saturn, Jupiter, Mars.
Literal seven-planet order, repeating continuously through day and night.
condition
continually during day and night
Planetary rulers run without resetting between daylight and nighttime.
The cycle changes ruler after each unequal hour.
source_example
Sunday first Sun
Lilly demonstrates a Sunday whose first hour is Sun.
Illustrative construction, not a real observed outcome.
source_example
Monday first Moon second Saturn third Jupiter fourth Mars
The uninterrupted seven-planet sequence results in Monday first Moon, then Saturn, Jupiter, Mars.
Follows previous Sunday cycle after 24 planetary hours.
method
24 hours from sunrise until next sunrise
Lilly accounts twenty-four planetary hours from one sunrise to the next.
Twelve daytime and twelve nighttime segments.
source_qualification
begin evermore Sun-rise
The hourly count always begins with the weekday's planet at sunrise.
Depends on daily sunrise; the claim cannot be replaced with a fixed clock.

label: Unequal astrological hours versus constant sixty-minute civil hours
claims: authorial_context
Ancients Winter and Summer equal hours
Lilly notes that some earlier authorities used equal 60-minute hours for day and night even in winter and summer.
Attributed rival method, not Lilly's accepted one.
method
Astrologians follow motion of Sun
He rejects constant-duration hours in favor of sunlight-dependent lengths.
The source requires solar times, not merely the weekday.
condition
Sun-rise to Sun-set twelve equal parts
The interval from sunrise to sunset is divided into exactly twelve equal daylight parts.
Equal within one day, usually unequal to civil hours.
condition
one half before Noon
Lilly describes six daylight planetary hours before noon.
His printed table separates first and second six hours.
condition
rest after Noon
Six remaining daylight planetary hours fall after noon.
Noon division assumes his table's solar convention.
condition
Sun-set until next Sun-rise twelve parts
The next night from sunset to sunrise is likewise divided into twelve equal nighttime parts.
Nighttime planetary hour length generally differs from daylight length.
source_qualification
more or less sixty minutes
Throughout most of the year a planetary hour can be longer or shorter than sixty minutes.
This is an arithmetic observation, not empirical astrology validation.
condition
Sun into Aries or Libra sixty minutes
Lilly says planetary-hour duration becomes exactly sixty minutes at solar ingress into Aries or Libra.
Equinox idealization; no modern local astronomical parity asserted.
source_continuation
and so numbring until next day
The instruction to keep cycling from sunrise continues on the next printed page.
Original physical PDF516-to-517 source seam, no duplicate passage.

method

method

method
night latter six signs pages 7-8

method
Day planetary hour and night two different page pairs

Sign routing does not itself determine the hour ruler.
source_qualification
if Sun in sign not written in first column look opposite
Lilly allows using the complementary solar-sign rows printed along the opposite table margin.
The second margin is meaningful, not decorative.
